Fabricated on advanced logic wafers (5–7nm) for the highest-performance designs, with CoWoS or similar advanced packaging for some next-gen architectures.
Broadcom (Memory line) dominates with ~75% market share; Nvidia (Spectrum), Intel (Tofino), and Cisco (Silicon One) compete.
AI GPU clusters require non-blocking, ultra-low-latency switching fabrics — each cluster of 10,000+ GPUs needs hundreds of high-radix switches.
Switch ASICs are the traffic controllers of AI networking — every byte of training data and model gradient flows through these chips.

Optical Transceivers.name: Optical Transceivers
Optical Transceivers.about: Pluggable 800G/1.6T modules converting electrical signals to light for fiber links.
ai_summary: Modules that convert electrical signals to light and back — plugged into switches and servers to send data over fiber optic cable at 400G, 800G, or 1.6T speeds.
Inside each transceiver are InP or GaAs laser diodes, photodetectors, driver ICs, and a DSP chip — all packaged into a small pluggable module.
The AI transceiver market grew 57% to $26B in 2026; McKinsey projects 800G production will fall 40–60% short of demand through 2027.
Each AI GPU rack requires dozens of transceivers — a 10,000-GPU cluster can consume 50,000+ modules at 800G speeds.
Optical transceivers are the bandwidth bottleneck between compute and network — InP laser supply is the constraint behind the constraint.

Co-Packaged Optics.name: Co-Packaged Optics
Co-Packaged Optics.descriptor_pill: Optical engines integrated onto switch package, replacing...
Co-Packaged Optics.about: Optical engines integrated onto switch package, replacing pluggables for power efficiency.
ai_summary: Optical engines integrated directly into the switch ASIC package rather than plugged in externally — eliminating the electrical bottleneck between chip and fiber.
Combines silicon photonics, InP lasers, and advanced packaging onto a single substrate — a convergence of semiconductor and optical manufacturing.
Broadcom, Nvidia, and Ayar Labs are developing CPO architectures — early deployments expected in 2026–2027 AI cluster builds.
CPO reduces power consumption per bit by 30–50% compared to pluggable transceivers — meaningful at the scale of a 100,000-GPU cluster.
Co-packaged optics is the next-generation interconnect architecture for AI clusters — when it arrives at scale, it reshapes both networking and packaging supply chains.

Photonic ICs.name: Photonic ICs
Photonic ICs.descriptor_pill: Silicon photonics chips with heterogeneously-integrated I...
Photonic ICs.about: Silicon photonics chips with heterogeneously-integrated InP lasers for high-bandwidth optical I/O.
ai_summary: Silicon chips that guide, modulate, and detect light on a semiconductor substrate — the optical equivalent of an electronic integrated circuit.
Fabricated in silicon photonics fabs using 300mm wafers and modified CMOS processes — GlobalFoundries and TSMC offer silicon photonics foundry services.
Used inside advanced optical transceivers and co-packaged optics modules to replace discrete optical components with integrated waveguides.
Each 1.6T transceiver generation uses more silicon photonics content as the industry moves from discrete lasers to integrated optical engines.
Photonic ICs are the technology bridge between electronics and optics — still early in adoption but growing fast as AI bandwidth demands outrun electrical interconnects.

Network Switches.name: Network Switches
Network Switches.descriptor_pill: Assembled switch boxes routing rack-to-rack and building-...
Network Switches.about: Assembled switch boxes routing rack-to-rack and building-to-building traffic.
ai_summary: Box-level networking equipment containing switch ASICs, transceivers, power supplies, and cooling — the physical nodes that route data through datacenter networks.
Assembled from upstream switch ASICs (Broadcom/Nvidia), optical transceivers, FR-4 PCBs, and standard power/cooling components.
Arista, Cisco, and white-box ODMs (Edgecore, Celestica) supply datacenter switches — Arista leads in hyperscale AI cluster deployments.
A 10,000-GPU AI cluster requires hundreds of leaf and spine switches in a non-blocking fat-tree topology — each switch carries 32–64 high-speed ports.
Network switches are the assembled product where silicon, optics, and packaging converge — supply tracks the AI GPU buildout with a slight lag.

Fiber Optic Cable.name: Fiber Optic Cable
Fiber Optic Cable.descriptor_pill: Glass strands doped with germanium carrying optical signa...
Fiber Optic Cable.about: Glass strands doped with germanium carrying optical signals between racks, buildings, and continents.
ai_summary: Glass strands that carry data as pulses of light — the physical layer connecting every server, switch, and building in a datacenter campus.
Germanium-doped silica preforms are drawn into hair-thin fibers, coated with UV polymer, and bundled into cables — upstream constraints include GeCl₄, helium, and preform equipment.
Corning controls ~40% of Western fiber capacity; fiber prices surged 70%+ since late 2025 with lead times stretching to nearly a year for smaller customers.
AI-optimized datacenters consume 5–10x more fiber than conventional facilities; Nvidia Blackwell racks require 16x more fiber than traditional cloud switches.
Fiber is the physical bandwidth layer that everything else depends on — the shortage is real, structural, and getting worse as AI datacenter construction accelerates.

DACs & AECs.name: DACs & AECs
DACs & AECs.descriptor_pill: Direct-attach copper and active electrical cables for sho...
DACs & AECs.about: Direct-attach copper and active electrical cables for short-reach in-rack connections.
ai_summary: Direct attach copper cables and active electrical cables — short-reach connections (<5m) between adjacent switches and servers using copper instead of fiber.
DACs are passive copper twinax cables; AECs add a small active chip at each end to boost signal integrity over slightly longer distances.
Cheaper than optical transceivers for short-reach connections — each 400G DAC costs $100–200 versus $500–1,000 for an optical transceiver.
Used within racks and between adjacent racks where distances are short enough for copper — AI clusters use a mix of DACs (short) and optics (long).
DACs reduce the optical transceiver count in dense GPU clusters — a cost optimization that matters when a cluster needs tens of thousands of links.

NICs / DPUs.name: NICs / DPUs
NICs / DPUs.descriptor_pill: Network interface and data processing units offloading ne...
NICs / DPUs.about: Network interface and data processing units offloading networking and storage work from CPUs.
ai_summary: Network interface cards and data processing units that offload networking, security, and storage tasks from the host CPU so it doesn't get bogged down.
Built on mature-node logic wafers and packaged with standard substrates — less advanced fabrication than GPUs but essential for system efficiency.
Nvidia (ConnectX/BlueField), Broadcom, and Intel/Marvell are the main suppliers — Nvidia's DPUs are increasingly bundled with GPU server platforms.
Each AI server typically has 1–2 NICs/DPUs; large GPU clusters require hundreds per rack for RDMA networking at 400G–800G speeds.
DPUs are becoming the third processor in every AI server alongside GPU and CPU — a growing silicon demand vector that competes for fab capacity.

Coolant Distribution Units.name: Coolant Distribution Units
Coolant Distribution Units.descriptor_pill: Pumps, heat exchangers, and controls circulating coolant ...
Coolant Distribution Units.about: Pumps, heat exchangers, and controls circulating coolant from chillers to rack manifolds.
ai_summary: Rack-mounted or row-level units that regulate temperature, pressure, and flow rate of liquid coolant distributed to server cold plates — the control layer of liquid cooling.
Takes facility chilled water or coolant from a central plant and distributes it at precise temperature and flow rates to individual server racks.
Vertiv, CoolIT, and Motivair are leading CDU suppliers — the market is scaling rapidly as liquid cooling becomes mandatory for AI GPU racks.
Each AI rack drawing 40–120 kW requires a CDU — datacenter operators are retrofitting existing facilities and designing new ones around liquid cooling from day one.
CDUs are the control interface between facility cooling infrastructure and the servers — the component that makes precision liquid cooling manageable at datacenter scale.

Manifolds & QDs.name: Manifolds & QDs
Manifolds & QDs.descriptor_pill: In-rack flow distribution and quick-disconnect fittings s...
Manifolds & QDs.about: In-rack flow distribution and quick-disconnect fittings serving each compute tray.
ai_summary: Plumbing manifolds and quick-disconnect fittings that connect liquid cooling loops to individual servers — allowing hot-swap of servers without draining the cooling system.
Quick disconnects use dripless valve mechanisms that seal when disconnected, preventing coolant leaks during server maintenance — a mechanical precision component.
CPC (Colder Products), Staubli, and Parker supply QD fittings; manifold designs are typically custom to the rack architecture.
Every liquid-cooled server in an AI rack connects through QD fittings — a 72-GPU rack might have 70+ individual quick-disconnect connections.
Manifolds and QDs are the mechanical interface that makes liquid cooling practical for server maintenance — without dripless disconnects, every swap risks a coolant spill.

Chillers.name: Chillers
Chillers.descriptor_pill: Air- or water-cooled chillers rejecting facility heat fro...
Chillers.about: Air- or water-cooled chillers rejecting facility heat from secondary loops.
ai_summary: Refrigeration units that remove heat from datacenter coolant loops and reject it to the outdoor environment — the thermal workhorse of every large facility.
Use refrigerant compression-expansion cycles to transfer heat from ~10–15°C chilled water supply to outdoor ambient — consuming significant electricity in the process.
Trane (Ingersoll Rand), Carrier (now part of Honeywell), Johnson Controls, and Daikin are leading chiller manufacturers.
A 100 MW datacenter typically requires 30–50 MW of chiller capacity — cooling is the largest non-IT power consumer in traditional air-cooled facilities.
Chiller efficiency (measured in kW/ton) directly affects datacenter PUE — every improvement in chiller COP reduces the total facility power draw.

Cooling Towers.name: Cooling Towers
Cooling Towers.descriptor_pill: Evaporative or dry coolers rejecting heat to atmosphere, ...
Cooling Towers.about: Evaporative or dry coolers rejecting heat to atmosphere, often paired with adiabatic assist.
ai_summary: Outdoor heat rejection systems that evaporate water to cool the warm condenser water returning from chillers — the final thermal link between datacenter heat and the atmosphere.
Warm water from the chiller condenser is sprayed over fill media while fans draw air through — evaporation cools the water, which recirculates back to the chiller.
SPX Cooling, BAC, and Evapco are major cooling tower manufacturers — designs range from small rooftop units to large field-erected towers.
A 100 MW datacenter can evaporate 1–5 million gallons of water per day through its cooling towers, depending on climate and cooling architecture.
Cooling towers are where datacenter energy consumption meets water consumption — the tradeoff between water use and energy efficiency is a siting-level decision.

CRAH / Fan Wall Units.name: CRAH / Fan Wall Units
CRAH / Fan Wall Units.descriptor_pill: Air-handling units cooling residual loads from networking...
CRAH / Fan Wall Units.about: Air-handling units cooling residual loads from networking, storage, and ancillary equipment.
ai_summary: Computer room air handlers that blow conditioned air through raised floors or overhead ducts to cool server racks — the traditional cooling delivery method for air-cooled datacenters.
Contain fans driven by NdFeB magnet motors, cooling coils fed by chilled water, and filters — each unit handles 50–200 kW of heat removal.
Vertiv (Liebert), Schneider Electric (APC), and Stulz are leading CRAH manufacturers.
AI datacenters are transitioning away from air-cooled CRAHs toward liquid cooling, but most existing facilities and lower-density zones still rely on them.
Fan wall designs (multiple smaller fans vs. one large fan) improve redundancy and efficiency — the design evolution reflects the industry's shift toward higher rack densities.

Heat Exchangers.name: Heat Exchangers
Heat Exchangers.about: Plate-and-frame and shell-and-tube exchangers transferring heat between facility loops.
ai_summary: Metal devices that transfer heat between two fluid streams without mixing them — used throughout datacenter cooling systems to isolate loops and manage temperatures.
Plate, shell-and-tube, and microchannel designs are used depending on application — stainless steel and copper-nickel alloys are common construction materials.
Alfa Laval, Kelvion, and GEA are leading heat exchanger manufacturers — commodity equipment with well-established supply chains.
Datacenters use heat exchangers between chilled water loops, between coolant circuits and building water, and in free-cooling economizer systems.
Heat exchangers are thermal infrastructure plumbing — widely available, not constrained, but essential to every cooling architecture.

MV Switchgear.name: MV Switchgear
MV Switchgear.descriptor_pill: Medium-voltage breakers, relays, and metering routing uti...
MV Switchgear.about: Medium-voltage breakers, relays, and metering routing utility/onsite power inside the facility.
ai_summary: Medium-voltage (5–35 kV) switching equipment that connects the utility feed to a datacenter's internal distribution system — the first point of electrical control inside the facility.
Contains circuit breakers, bus bars, instrument transformers, and protective relaying — housed in metal-enclosed compartments rated for arc-flash containment.
Eaton, Schneider Electric, ABB (now Hitachi Energy), and Siemens are leading switchgear manufacturers.
Each datacenter utility feed requires MV switchgear; a 100+ MW campus may have multiple switchgear lineups for redundancy and segmentation.
MV switchgear lead times have stretched to 40–60 weeks, tracking the same transformer and electrical equipment delivery bottleneck constraining datacenter energization.

Step-Down Transformers.name: Step-Down Transformers
Step-Down Transformers.descriptor_pill: Pad-mount three-phase transformers stepping MV to 415V fo...
Step-Down Transformers.about: Pad-mount three-phase transformers stepping MV to 415V for IT and facility loads.
ai_summary: Power transformers that reduce high-voltage utility supply (69–230 kV) to the medium voltage (13–35 kV) used inside datacenter distribution systems.
Core is made from grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES), wound with copper or aluminum conductors, and immersed in insulating transformer oil.
ABB/Hitachi Energy, Siemens, and Virginia Transformer are major suppliers — lead times have stretched to 2–3 years driven by GOES shortages and surging orders.
Every datacenter substation requires step-down transformers — a 100 MW facility typically needs 3–6 large transformers for the main feeds.
Transformer delivery is one of the most binding physical constraints on datacenter energization — the GOES steel shortage flows directly into datacenter timelines.

UPS Systems.name: UPS Systems
UPS Systems.descriptor_pill: Static double-conversion units providing instantaneous ba...
UPS Systems.about: Static double-conversion units providing instantaneous backup until generators come online.
ai_summary: Uninterruptible power supply units that provide instant battery-backed power during the gap between utility failure and generator startup — typically 10–30 seconds of ride-through.
Contain battery banks (lithium-ion or VRLA), power electronics (inverters/rectifiers built from mature-node silicon), and control systems.
Vertiv, Schneider Electric (APC), and Eaton dominate the datacenter UPS market — large 500+ kW systems are standard for AI deployments.
Every AI server rack is fed through a UPS to prevent data loss and hardware damage during power transitions.
UPS systems are transitioning from lead-acid to lithium-ion batteries, reducing footprint and improving efficiency — but adding another lithium demand vector.

BESS.name: BESS
BESS.descriptor_pill: Containerized 5 MWh+ battery systems for longer-duration ...
BESS.about: Containerized 5 MWh+ battery systems for longer-duration backup and grid services.
ai_summary: Battery energy storage systems — containerized banks of LFP cells that provide minutes-to-hours of backup power and grid services for datacenters.
Built from LFP battery cells stacked into modules, connected to inverters and thermal management, and packaged in shipping containers for deployment.
CATL, BYD, Tesla (Megapack), and Sungrow are leading BESS integrators — Chinese cell dominance extends through the assembled system.
Hyperscalers are deploying 100+ MWh BESS installations at datacenter campuses — replacing diesel generators for short-duration backup and providing grid arbitrage.
BESS is the enabling technology for datacenters in grid-constrained locations — it smooths intermittent renewables and provides power during outages without diesel.

Vanadium Redox Flow Batteries.name: Vanadium Redox Flow Batteries
Vanadium Redox Flow Batteries.descriptor_pill: Long-duration storage pairing with renewables; emerging a...
Vanadium Redox Flow Batteries.about: Long-duration storage pairing with renewables; emerging alternative to lithium for 8+ hour discharge.
stats: Invinity Energy, Sumitomo Electric, VRB Energy
ai_summary: Long-duration energy storage systems where energy is stored in liquid vanadium electrolyte pumped through electrode stacks — discharge duration scales with tank size, not stack size.
Unlike lithium-ion, the vanadium electrolyte doesn't degrade over charge cycles — the system can cycle daily for 25+ years without capacity fade.
Invinity Energy Systems, Rongke Power, and CellCube are leading VRFB manufacturers — still a small market compared to lithium-ion BESS.
VRFBs are suited for 4–12 hour discharge applications at datacenter campuses — smoothing solar intermittency and providing longer backup than lithium-ion.
Flow batteries trade power density for longevity — if long-duration storage becomes standard at datacenter sites, VRFBs offer a cost-competitive alternative to lithium-ion degradation.

Automatic Transfer Switches.name: Automatic Transfer Switches
Automatic Transfer Switches.descriptor_pill: Source-switching gear handing over between utility, gener...
Automatic Transfer Switches.about: Source-switching gear handing over between utility, generator, and UPS during disruptions.
ai_summary: Electrical switches that detect utility power loss and automatically transfer load to backup generators or battery systems within seconds — the failover mechanism for datacenter power.
Monitor incoming utility voltage and frequency continuously; when parameters fall outside tolerance, the ATS transfers load to the backup source in 10–30 seconds.
ASCO (Schneider Electric), Eaton, and Generac supply ATS equipment — standard industrial products with well-established supply chains.
Every Tier III and Tier IV datacenter has multiple ATS units providing automatic failover between utility feeds and backup generators.
ATS equipment is standard electrical infrastructure — not supply-constrained and not a chokepoint, but structurally required in every datacenter.

PDUs & Rack PDUs.name: PDUs & Rack PDUs
PDUs & Rack PDUs.descriptor_pill: Distribute conditioned power from facility level down to ...
PDUs & Rack PDUs.about: Distribute conditioned power from facility level down to individual rack receptacles.
ai_summary: Power distribution units that step down facility-level power to rack-level voltages and route it to individual servers with metering and switching capability.
Floor PDUs transform medium-voltage to rack-level; rack PDUs distribute power to individual server power supplies with per-outlet monitoring.
Vertiv, Schneider Electric, and Server Technology (now Legrand) supply rack PDUs — standard equipment with short lead times.
Each AI server rack has 1–2 rack PDUs; large GPU racks running 40–120 kW require high-amperage PDU designs with busbar distribution.
Rack PDUs are commodity electrical distribution — supply is adequate and not a bottleneck.

Busways & Busbars.name: Busways & Busbars
Busways & Busbars.descriptor_pill: Overhead copper or aluminum distribution running power al...
Busways & Busbars.about: Overhead copper or aluminum distribution running power along rack rows.
ai_summary: Prefabricated copper or aluminum conductors enclosed in insulated housings — used to distribute power from floor PDUs to rack rows without running individual cable bundles.
Copper busbar is the preferred conductor for high-density AI deployments due to lower resistance and smaller cross-section at high currents.
Starline, Schneider Electric, and ABB supply overhead busway systems — increasingly specified for AI datacenter designs where rack power exceeds 30 kW.
Busway replaces cable trays in high-density zones, reducing installation time and improving serviceability — each tap-off box feeds a rack PDU.
Busways are a design choice that scales with rack power density — as AI pushes racks above 50 kW, busway distribution becomes the preferred topology.

Backup Generators.name: Backup Generators
Backup Generators.descriptor_pill: Diesel and gas gensets providing extended-runtime backup ...
Backup Generators.about: Diesel and gas gensets providing extended-runtime backup during utility outages.
ai_summary: Diesel or natural gas reciprocating engine generator sets that provide emergency power during extended utility outages — the last-resort power source for every datacenter.
Typically Caterpillar or Cummins diesel gensets rated 2–3 MW each, starting automatically via ATS when utility power fails.
Lead times for large diesel gensets stretched to 30–50 weeks in 2024–2025 as datacenter orders competed with grid resilience and disaster recovery demand.
Tier III datacenters require N+1 generator redundancy; a 100 MW facility typically has 40–60 generators with 24–72 hours of diesel fuel onsite.
Diesel generators are being supplemented by BESS and gas turbines for new AI datacenters, but remain the universal backup standard in existing facilities.

LV/MV Cable.name: LV/MV Cable
LV/MV Cable.descriptor_pill: Insulated copper or aluminum power cabling distributing e...
LV/MV Cable.about: Insulated copper or aluminum power cabling distributing electricity throughout the facility.
ai_summary: Low-voltage and medium-voltage copper or aluminum cables with XLPE insulation — the physical power delivery paths connecting substations to server racks.
Copper cable is preferred for high-current AI rack feeds; aluminum is used for longer distribution runs where weight and cost matter more than current density.
Prysmian, Nexans, Southwire, and Belden supply datacenter power cable — standard industrial products with generally adequate supply.
A 100 MW datacenter may contain hundreds of kilometers of power cable across MV feeders, LV distribution, and rack-level wiring.
Cable supply is generally adequate — the constraint is more often conduit space, installation labor, and the upstream copper/aluminum material than the cable itself.

Frame Gas Turbines.name: Frame Gas Turbines
Frame Gas Turbines.descriptor_pill: H- and F-class utility-scale turbines (140–600 MW) for pr...
Frame Gas Turbines.about: H- and F-class utility-scale turbines (140–600 MW) for primary on-campus power.
stats: GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi Power
ai_summary: Large industrial gas turbines (50–500+ MW) that burn natural gas to generate electricity — the fastest path to GW-scale onsite power for AI datacenter campuses.
Contain nickel superalloy turbine blades (using rhenium, hafnium, tungsten), GOES transformer steel, and complex combustion systems.
GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, and Mitsubishi Power are the three dominant frame turbine manufacturers globally.
Combined-cycle gas turbine plants can deliver 500+ MW within 18–24 months — faster than nuclear, more reliable than renewables alone.
Frame gas turbines are the bridge power technology for the first wave of GW-scale AI datacenters — the question is whether gas remains the default or transitions to nuclear.

Aeroderivative Turbines.name: Aeroderivative Turbines
Aeroderivative Turbines.about: Jet-engine-derived 30–70 MW turbines (e.g., LM2500) deployed at Stargate for fast ramp.
stats: GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Solar Turbines
ai_summary: Gas turbines adapted from aircraft jet engines — lighter, faster-starting, and more flexible than frame turbines but typically smaller (20–100 MW).
Derived from proven aero engine designs (GE LM2500, Rolls-Royce MT30), adapted with industrial generators and control systems for power generation.
GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, and Rolls-Royce Power Systems supply aeroderivative units — fewer manufacturers than frame turbines.
Start in minutes rather than hours, making them suited for peaking power, grid balancing, and rapid deployment at datacenter sites.
Aeroderivative turbines fill the gap between battery backup (minutes) and frame turbine baseload (months to build) — flexible power for phased datacenter growth.

Reciprocating Gas Engines.name: Reciprocating Gas Engines
Reciprocating Gas Engines.descriptor_pill: 3–20 MW modular gas engines providing fast-start power an...
Reciprocating Gas Engines.about: 3–20 MW modular gas engines providing fast-start power and transient load following.
ai_summary: Internal combustion engines running on natural gas that generate 1–20 MW each — typically deployed in clusters for distributed datacenter power.
Simpler than gas turbines, with higher electrical efficiency at partial loads — well-suited for modular datacenter deployments that scale incrementally.
Caterpillar (MaK), Wärtsilä, and Jenbacher (Innio) are leading manufacturers — established industrial products with 20–30 week lead times.
Some datacenter operators deploy recip engine plants for onsite generation, particularly in locations where gas pipeline access is available but grid capacity isn't.
Reciprocating engines are the low-complexity option for onsite datacenter power — less efficient than combined-cycle turbines but faster to deploy and easier to scale.

Solar PV Modules.name: Solar PV Modules
Solar PV Modules.descriptor_pill: Crystalline silicon or CdTe panels providing renewable su...
Solar PV Modules.about: Crystalline silicon or CdTe panels providing renewable supply, often paired with BESS.
ai_summary: Flat panels containing silicon solar cells that convert sunlight to DC electricity — the most widely deployed renewable power technology for datacenter supply.
Built from solar silicon wafers, silver conductive paste, tempered solar glass, EVA encapsulant, and aluminum frames — China produces ~80% of global modules.
Module prices have fallen below $0.10/W in 2025 — so cheap that the installation labor and balance-of-system costs now dominate total solar project economics.
Hyperscalers are signing multi-GW solar PPAs to power AI datacenters — each GW of solar requires ~2 million panels across ~5,000 acres.
Solar modules are abundant and cheap, but the land, interconnection, and grid capacity required to deploy them at datacenter scale are the real constraints.

Solar Inverters.name: Solar Inverters
Solar Inverters.descriptor_pill: String and central inverters converting DC PV output to g...
Solar Inverters.about: String and central inverters converting DC PV output to grid-compatible AC.
ai_summary: Power electronics that convert DC output from solar panels into grid-compatible AC electricity — the electrical interface between solar array and datacenter.
Contain GaN or SiC power transistors, magnetics, and digital control systems — efficiency exceeds 98% in modern string and central inverter designs.
Huawei, Sungrow, SMA, and Enphase are leading inverter suppliers — Huawei faces trade restrictions in some Western markets.
Each MW of solar capacity requires inverter capacity to match — a 100 MW solar farm needs ~100 MW of inverter capacity.
Inverters are a mature, competitive market with adequate supply — the constraint on solar-powered datacenters is interconnection and grid capacity, not inverter availability.

Solar Racking & Trackers.name: Solar Racking & Trackers
Solar Racking & Trackers.descriptor_pill: Steel mounting structures and single-axis trackers positi...
Solar Racking & Trackers.about: Steel mounting structures and single-axis trackers positioning PV modules toward the sun.
ai_summary: Steel and aluminum structures that hold solar panels at the correct angle to the sun — fixed-tilt racks for rooftop and single-axis trackers for ground-mount utility-scale.
Single-axis trackers (Nextracker, Array Technologies) follow the sun east-to-west, boosting energy yield by 15–25% versus fixed-tilt installations.
Built from galvanized steel, aluminum extrusions, and electric motors (with NdFeB magnets in the tracker drives) — structural steel is the dominant material input.
A 100 MW ground-mount solar farm requires ~2,000–3,000 tonnes of steel racking or tracker structure.
Racking and trackers are commodity structural products — supply is adequate and not a meaningful constraint on solar deployment for datacenters.

Wind Turbines.name: Wind Turbines
Wind Turbines.descriptor_pill: Onshore turbines occasionally co-located with datacenter ...
Wind Turbines.about: Onshore turbines occasionally co-located with datacenter campuses (e.g., Abilene region).
ai_summary: Multi-MW generators with 80–170m rotor diameters that convert wind energy to electricity — used in onshore and offshore wind farms that supply datacenter power via PPA.
Contain NdFeB permanent magnets in direct-drive generators (or gearboxes in geared designs), fiberglass blades, steel towers, and copper wiring.
Vestas, Siemens Gamesa, GE Vernova, and Goldwind are leading turbine manufacturers — the industry has been in margin compression since 2022.
Several hyperscalers have signed wind PPAs to power AI datacenters, particularly in the US Midwest and Northern Europe where wind resources are strong.
Wind turbine supply is adequate but the NdFeB magnets inside direct-drive generators tie turbine delivery to the same Chinese rare earth export controls affecting other parts of the chain.

Small Modular Reactors.name: Small Modular Reactors
Small Modular Reactors.descriptor_pill: Factory-built 50–350 MW reactors emerging as long-duratio...
Small Modular Reactors.about: Factory-built 50–350 MW reactors emerging as long-duration clean baseload for AI campuses.
ai_summary: Factory-fabricated nuclear reactors producing 50–300 MW of electricity — designed for faster permitting, lower capital cost, and modular deployment near AI datacenter loads.
Designs from X-energy (Xe-100, pebble bed), Kairos Power (KP-FHR, molten salt), TerraPower (Natrium, sodium-cooled), and NuScale (VOYGR, light water) are furthest along.
Most SMR designs require HALEU fuel (5–20% enriched uranium) that doesn't exist at commercial scale outside Russia — the binding fuel supply constraint.
Microsoft, Google, and Amazon have all announced SMR partnerships for datacenter power, but no commercial SMR operates in the US as of 2026.
SMRs are the long-term clean baseload power solution for AI datacenters — the question is whether fuel supply, permitting, and construction timelines align with the pace of AI demand.

Conventional Nuclear.name: Conventional Nuclear
Conventional Nuclear.descriptor_pill: Recommissioned or extended large reactors supplying datac...
Conventional Nuclear.about: Recommissioned or extended large reactors supplying datacenter PPAs (e.g., Three Mile Island).
ai_summary: Existing light-water reactor fleet (~440 units globally, ~93 in the US) generating ~370 GW of zero-carbon baseload electricity — the only proven large-scale clean power source.
Uses LEU fuel (3–5% enriched), cooled and moderated by water, with zircaloy-clad fuel assemblies and a containment structure — mature, well-understood technology.
Constellation Energy, NextEra, and EDF operate the largest Western nuclear fleets — Microsoft's Three Mile Island restart made datacenter nuclear procurement mainstream.
Nuclear plants offer 90%+ capacity factors and zero carbon — the most reliable power source for 24/7 AI workloads.
The nuclear fleet restart for AI power is already underway — the constraint is reactor availability and grid proximity, not technology or fuel supply.

Fuel Cells.name: Fuel Cells
Fuel Cells.descriptor_pill: Solid-oxide cells providing distributed onsite power, dep...
Fuel Cells.about: Solid-oxide cells providing distributed onsite power, deployed at hyperscale sites like Stargate.
stats: Bloom Energy, FuelCell Energy, Plug Power
ai_summary: Electrochemical devices that convert fuel (natural gas, hydrogen, biogas) directly to electricity without combustion — achieving 40–60% electrical efficiency.
Solid oxide fuel cells (Bloom Energy) run at ~1,000°C using a YSZ electrolyte; PEM fuel cells run at ~80°C using a platinum catalyst membrane.
Bloom Energy is the leading SOFC supplier for datacenter applications, with installations at Apple, Google, and Equinix facilities.
Fuel cells provide onsite power with lower emissions than gas turbines and can run on hydrogen when available — a bridge to fully clean power.
Fuel cells offer datacenter operators power without grid dependency — relevant for sites where grid interconnection is years away but gas pipeline access exists.

Generator Step-Up Transformers.name: Generator Step-Up Transformers
Generator Step-Up Transformers.descriptor_pill: Large transformers stepping plant output up to transmissi...
Generator Step-Up Transformers.about: Large transformers stepping plant output up to transmission voltage; 144-week lead times.
stats: Hitachi Energy, GE Vernova, Hyundai Electric
ai_summary: Large power transformers that increase generator output voltage from 11–25 kV to the 69–345 kV level needed for transmission — required at every onsite power plant.
Same GOES core, copper windings, and transformer oil construction as step-down transformers — subject to the same 2–3 year lead times.
ABB/Hitachi Energy, Siemens, and GE Vernova supply GSUs — the same manufacturers facing the global transformer delivery bottleneck.
Every gas turbine, nuclear plant, or large solar farm supplying a datacenter needs a GSU to feed power into the transmission grid.
GSU transformers are part of the same GOES-constrained delivery pipeline as step-down transformers — another transformer bottleneck in the datacenter power chain.

HV Switchgear & Breakers.name: HV Switchgear & Breakers
HV Switchgear & Breakers.descriptor_pill: High-voltage substation gear protecting and isolating tra...
HV Switchgear & Breakers.about: High-voltage substation gear protecting and isolating transmission interconnects.
ai_summary: High-voltage (69–345 kV) switching and protection equipment at the grid interface — circuit breakers, disconnect switches, and bus configurations that control power flow.
Contains SF₆ or C4-FN insulating gas, copper bus conductors, and protective relay systems — large, heavy equipment fabricated by a few global manufacturers.
ABB/Hitachi Energy, Siemens, and GE Vernova supply HV switchgear — lead times of 40–80 weeks, tracking the broader electrical equipment delivery bottleneck.
Each utility interconnection point and onsite power plant at a datacenter campus requires HV switchgear for protection and isolation.
HV switchgear delivery is another electrical equipment lead-time constraint — part of the same equipment delivery challenge as transformers and MV gear.

HV Transmission Cable.name: HV Transmission Cable
HV Transmission Cable.descriptor_pill: Overhead conductor and underground HVDC cables connecting...
HV Transmission Cable.about: Overhead conductor and underground HVDC cables connecting plants to load.
ai_summary: High-voltage (69–345 kV) cable using XLPE insulation and copper or aluminum conductors — used for underground transmission connecting substations to datacenters.
Underground transmission avoids the permitting challenges of overhead lines but costs 5–10x more per kilometer.
Prysmian, Nexans, and Southwire manufacture HV cable — lead times of 30–50 weeks for custom long-run orders.
Datacenters in urban or suburban locations often require underground HV transmission because overhead lines face siting opposition.
HV cable is a specialized product with adequate manufacturing capacity — the constraint is more often right-of-way permitting than cable supply.

Selective Catalytic Reduction.name: Selective Catalytic Reduction
Selective Catalytic Reduction.descriptor_pill: Emissions control reducing NOx output from gas turbines t...
Selective Catalytic Reduction.about: Emissions control reducing NOx output from gas turbines to permit-compliant levels.
ai_summary: Exhaust treatment system that injects urea solution into gas turbine or engine exhaust to reduce nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions to regulatory limits.
Contains a catalyst bed (vanadium or zeolite-based) and an aqueous urea injection system — required for air quality permitting in most US jurisdictions.
Johnson Matthey, BASF, and Cummins Emission Solutions supply SCR systems — standard industrial air quality equipment.
Every gas turbine and many reciprocating engines at a datacenter power plant require SCR to meet local emissions standards.
SCR is a permitting prerequisite rather than a supply constraint — without it, gas-fired datacenter power plants can't get air quality permits.

Heat Recovery Steam Generators.name: Heat Recovery Steam Generators
Heat Recovery Steam Generators.descriptor_pill: Recover exhaust heat from gas turbines for combined-cycle...
Heat Recovery Steam Generators.about: Recover exhaust heat from gas turbines for combined-cycle efficiency gains.
ai_summary: Boilers that capture waste heat from gas turbine exhaust (~500–600°C) to generate steam that drives a secondary steam turbine — the 'combined cycle' that boosts plant efficiency from ~38% to ~60%.
Contains finned tube bundles, steam drums, and economizers — large pressure vessels fabricated by specialty boiler manufacturers.
Nooter/Eriksen, Vogt (now Babcock & Wilcox), and CMI Energy are leading HRSG manufacturers — lead times of 18–24 months.
The efficiency gain from adding an HRSG (combined cycle) reduces fuel cost per MWh by ~35% — meaningful for a GW-scale datacenter running 24/7.
HRSGs are what make gas-fired datacenter power economic at scale — the combined-cycle efficiency premium justifies the additional capital and construction time.

Structural Steel.name: Structural Steel
Structural Steel.descriptor_pill: Hot-rolled frame, decking, and plate carrying multi-story...
Structural Steel.about: Hot-rolled frame, decking, and plate carrying multi-story datacenter loads.
ai_summary: Hot-rolled steel beams, columns, and plates that form the primary load-bearing frame of datacenter buildings — the skeleton everything else hangs on.
Produced from iron ore in blast furnaces or from scrap steel in electric arc furnaces — EAF steel is increasingly preferred for lower carbon footprint.
Nucor, Steel Dynamics, and ArcelorMittal are major structural steel suppliers — US EAF capacity is growing.
A 100 MW datacenter building requires roughly 5,000–15,000 tonnes of structural steel depending on design and height.
Structural steel supply is generally adequate — the constraint on datacenter construction is more often labor, permitting, and power availability than steel.

Cold-Formed Steel.name: Cold-Formed Steel
Cold-Formed Steel.descriptor_pill: Lightweight studs, joists, and purlins for secondary fram...
Cold-Formed Steel.about: Lightweight studs, joists, and purlins for secondary framing and walls.
ai_summary: Thin-gauge steel bent and shaped at room temperature into studs, joists, and framing members — used for interior walls, mezzanines, and equipment supports in datacenters.
Made from galvanized steel coil (zinc-coated for corrosion resistance) cut and formed by roll-forming machines — a commodity construction product.
ClarkDietrich, Steel Technologies, and Nucor Building Systems supply cold-formed steel — widely available with short lead times.
Interior partitioning, cable tray supports, and equipment mounting in datacenters all use cold-formed steel framing.
Cold-formed steel is a bulk construction input — abundant, inexpensive, and not a supply chain constraint.

Concrete.name: Concrete
Concrete.descriptor_pill: Mass pours for foundations rated for ~1,875 kg/m² point l...
Concrete.about: Mass pours for foundations rated for ~1,875 kg/m² point loads from NVL72 racks.
ai_summary: Mixture of cement, aggregates, and water that hardens into the foundations, floors, and structural elements of every datacenter building.
Cement production generates ~8% of global CO₂ emissions — hyperscaler Scope 3 reporting is pushing adoption of low-carbon concrete mixes.
A 100 MW datacenter requires 50,000–100,000 cubic yards of concrete — foundations, server floor slabs, and cooling tower basins are the major pours.
Low-carbon alternatives (CarbonCure, Solidia, Holcim ECOPact) inject captured CO₂ or use supplementary cementitious materials to reduce embodied carbon.
Concrete is the literal foundation of every datacenter — not constrained by supply but increasingly constrained by sustainability requirements.

Rebar.name: Rebar
Rebar.descriptor_pill: Deformed steel bar reinforcing concrete foundations and s...
Rebar.about: Deformed steel bar reinforcing concrete foundations and slabs.
ai_summary: Reinforcing steel bars embedded in concrete to provide tensile strength — every concrete foundation, slab, and structural element in a datacenter contains rebar.
Produced from scrap steel in EAF mini-mills — the same domestic steel recycling loop that feeds structural steel production.
Nucor, CMC, and Gerdau are major US rebar producers — a commodity product with adequate supply and short lead times.
A large datacenter foundation pour can require thousands of tonnes of rebar, with epoxy-coated rebar specified for corrosion protection in below-grade applications.
Rebar is a commodity construction input — structurally essential but not a meaningful supply chain constraint.

Raised Flooring.name: Raised Flooring
Raised Flooring.descriptor_pill: Modular access floor system routing cabling, cooling, and...
Raised Flooring.about: Modular access floor system routing cabling, cooling, and power below the white space.
stats: Tate Access Floors, ASM Modular, Haworth
ai_summary: Modular floor tile system elevated 12–36 inches above the structural slab — creating a plenum for cable routing, air distribution, and coolant piping.
Tiles are typically steel-clad with cementitious fill, mounted on adjustable steel pedestals — the system allows flexible layout changes as IT loads evolve.
Tate (Kingspan), Haworth, and MERO supply raised floor systems — standard datacenter construction products with adequate availability.
Traditional air-cooled datacenters use the raised floor plenum for cold-air supply; liquid-cooled facilities use it primarily for cable and pipe management.
Raised flooring is being reconsidered as AI racks shift to overhead liquid cooling — some new builds eliminate the raised floor entirely.

Fire Suppression.name: Fire Suppression
Fire Suppression.descriptor_pill: Clean-agent (FM-200, Novec 1230) and water-mist systems p...
Fire Suppression.about: Clean-agent (FM-200, Novec 1230) and water-mist systems protecting IT and electrical rooms.
ai_summary: Gaseous and sprinkler-based systems that detect and extinguish fires in datacenter white space, electrical rooms, and generator enclosures without damaging equipment.
Clean agent systems (FM-200, inert gas blends) protect IT space; pre-action sprinklers protect lower-risk areas — both required for Tier III/IV compliance.
Johnson Controls (Tyco), Siemens, and Kidde (Carrier) are leading fire suppression suppliers.
The transition away from PFAS-based clean agents (Novec 1230) is adding cost and complexity — inert gas systems (IG-541, Argonite) are the primary replacement.
Fire suppression is a regulatory and insurance requirement — not a supply bottleneck but subject to the same PFAS-transition challenges as other fluorochemical products.

Security Systems.name: Security Systems
Security Systems.descriptor_pill: Fencing, access control, cameras, and intrusion detection...
Security Systems.about: Fencing, access control, cameras, and intrusion detection across the campus perimeter.
ai_summary: Cameras, access control, intrusion detection, and monitoring systems that protect datacenter physical perimeter and interior spaces.
Built from mature-node semiconductors, IP networking equipment, and software — standard commercial security technology deployed at higher density.
Honeywell, Bosch, and Axis Communications supply datacenter-grade physical security systems.
Hyperscale datacenters operate at government-grade physical security levels — mantraps, biometric access, 24/7 guard force, and continuous video monitoring.
Security systems are a required operational element — commodity technology not constrained by supply.

Land & Water Rights.name: Land & Water Rights
Land & Water Rights.descriptor_pill: 1,000+ acre parcels with water access and grid interconne...
Land & Water Rights.about: 1,000+ acre parcels with water access and grid interconnect rights for hypergrid campuses.
ai_summary: The physical land parcel and the legal right to use water at a datacenter site — the most fundamental non-technical input that determines where a datacenter can exist.
AI datacenter campus sites typically require 50–500+ acres with proximity to high-voltage transmission, fiber routes, and water supply.
Competition for datacenter-suitable land has driven site acquisition to rural areas in Virginia, Texas, Iowa, and the US Southeast.
Water rights are becoming a binding constraint in arid regions — a 100 MW air-cooled datacenter can consume 1–5 million gallons/day.
Land and water are the two inputs that cannot be manufactured, shipped, or substituted — they set the absolute physical boundary on where AI infrastructure can be built.

Advanced Logic Wafers.name: Advanced Logic Wafers
Advanced Logic Wafers.descriptor_pill: Patterned silicon wafers at 5nm/3nm/2nm nodes carrying GP...
Advanced Logic Wafers.about: Patterned silicon wafers at 5nm/3nm/2nm nodes carrying GPUs, CPUs, switch ASICs, and photonic ICs.
ai_summary: Silicon wafers that have been through an advanced chip fab (5nm or below) carrying GPU, CPU, or networking chip designs — hundreds of process steps turn a blank disc into a wafer of uncut dies.

Upstream inputs include electronic-grade silicon for the wafer itself, EUV and DUV photoresists for patterning, tungsten for interconnect plugs, hafnium for gate dielectrics, and multiple noble gases for etching and implantation.
Only TSMC, Samsung, and Intel can fabricate advanced logic at 5nm and below — TSMC holds ~60% of advanced node revenue.
Lead times for advanced wafer starts are 3–4 months, with capacity sold out through 2026 for AI-related designs.
Every AI accelerator, host CPU, switch ASIC, and networking chip starts as a pattern on one of these wafers.

Mature-Node Logic Wafers.name: Mature-Node Logic Wafers
Mature-Node Logic Wafers.descriptor_pill: Patterned silicon at 28nm and older for SSD controllers, ...
Mature-Node Logic Wafers.about: Patterned silicon at 28nm and older for SSD controllers, inverter controls, power management, and sensors.
ai_summary: Silicon wafers fabricated at older process nodes (28nm and above) carrying designs for power management, controllers, sensors, and analog chips — simpler to make but essential to every system.
Use the same silicon feedstock and DUV photoresists as advanced wafers but skip EUV lithography, which keeps cost per wafer much lower.
Produced by dozens of fabs worldwide including TSMC, UMC, GlobalFoundries, and Chinese foundries — far less concentrated than advanced nodes.
AI datacenters consume mature-node chips in power supplies, UPS controllers, SSD controllers, sensor arrays, and security systems — dozens per server rack.
Mature nodes are the invisible majority of the chip supply chain — less glamorous than leading-edge but structurally irreplaceable in every subsystem.

DRAM Wafers.name: DRAM Wafers
DRAM Wafers.descriptor_pill: Patterned memory wafers feeding both standalone DDR modul...
DRAM Wafers.about: Patterned memory wafers feeding both standalone DDR modules and HBM stacks.
ai_summary: Silicon wafers patterned with dynamic random-access memory circuits — the working memory that GPUs read and write during AI training and inference.
Upstream inputs include electronic-grade silicon, DUV photoresists, krypton and argon for etching, and ultra-pure water for cleaning between process steps.
Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron produce virtually all DRAM wafers globally — a three-player oligopoly.
HBM (high-bandwidth memory) stacks are built by bonding and stacking these DRAM wafers with through-silicon vias, then packaging them alongside GPUs.
Samsung and SK Hynix warn AI-driven memory shortages could last through 2027 as HBM demand absorbs wafer capacity that previously served commodity DRAM.

NAND Wafers.name: NAND Wafers
NAND Wafers.descriptor_pill: Patterned 200+ layer 3D NAND wafers; high-aspect-ratio et...
NAND Wafers.about: Patterned 200+ layer 3D NAND wafers; high-aspect-ratio etch limits scaling.
ai_summary: Silicon wafers with vertically stacked memory cells (200+ layers) that store data persistently — the flash memory inside every SSD in an AI datacenter.
Uses similar silicon and DUV chemistry as DRAM but with a radically different 3D structure where cells are stacked vertically rather than shrunk horizontally.
Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron, Kioxia, and Western Digital share the market — more diversified than DRAM but still concentrated in East Asia.
Every AI training job produces checkpoints and datasets stored on enterprise SSDs built from NAND flash — storage demand scales with model size.
NAND supply is currently less constrained than DRAM because 3D stacking adds capacity without requiring leading-edge lithography.

Solar Silicon Wafers.name: Solar Silicon Wafers
Solar Silicon Wafers.descriptor_pill: Sliced monocrystalline ingots feeding c-Si solar cells; ~...
Solar Silicon Wafers.about: Sliced monocrystalline ingots feeding c-Si solar cells; ~97% Chinese production.
ai_summary: Thin slices of solar-grade polysilicon crystallized into ingots and wire-sawn into wafers — the light-absorbing substrate inside most solar panels.
Upstream polysilicon is purified from metallurgical silicon using the Siemens process, then crystallized and sliced — China controls ~95% of wafer production.
LONGi, TCL Zhonghuan, and other Chinese manufacturers dominate global solar wafer output at prices that have pushed most non-Chinese producers out.
Solar panels made from these wafers are being deployed at GW scale to power AI datacenters, particularly in the US Southwest.
Solar wafer supply is abundant and cheap — the constraint in solar-powered datacenters is inverters, grid interconnection, and land, not the wafers themselves.

Electronic-Grade Silicon.name: Electronic-Grade Silicon
Electronic-Grade Silicon.descriptor_pill: 99.9999999%+ pure CZ-grown ingots and wafers for every ch...
Electronic-Grade Silicon.about: 99.9999999%+ pure CZ-grown ingots and wafers for every chip in the facility.
ai_summary: Ultra-high-purity silicon (9–11 nines, 99.999999999%) grown into single-crystal ingots and sliced into the wafers that become chips — the foundation of all semiconductor manufacturing.
Starts as metallurgical-grade silicon from quartz, gets converted to trichlorosilane gas, purified through distillation, and deposited as polysilicon before crystal growth.
Shin-Etsu, SUMCO, Siltronic, SK Siltron, and GlobalWafers produce virtually all 300mm electronic-grade wafers — a five-company oligopoly.
Every chip in an AI datacenter — GPUs, CPUs, DRAM, NAND, power ICs, controllers — starts as a slice of this material.
Wafer supply is tight but expanding — the constraint is more often in downstream fab capacity than in raw wafer availability.

Electronic-Grade Polysilicon.name: Electronic-Grade Polysilicon
Electronic-Grade Polysilicon.descriptor_pill: Ultra-high-purity polysilicon feedstock distinct from sol...
Electronic-Grade Polysilicon.about: Ultra-high-purity polysilicon feedstock distinct from solar grade; Siemens-process produced.
ai_summary: Hyper-pure polycrystalline silicon (9N+) produced by the Siemens process — the feedstock melted and crystallized into the single-crystal ingots that become chip wafers.
Made by reacting metallurgical silicon with hydrochloric acid to form trichlorosilane, then distilling it to extreme purity and depositing it as solid polysilicon rods.
Wacker, Hemlock, Tokuyama, and OCI dominate electronic-grade polysilicon — distinct from the solar-grade market where Chinese producers lead.
Electronic grade requires 100–1,000x higher purity than solar grade — the quality gap creates a separate, smaller, higher-margin market.
Supply is adequate for current chip demand but any large-scale shift in solar wafer purity requirements could compete for the same purification capacity.

Solar-Grade Polysilicon.name: Solar-Grade Polysilicon
Solar-Grade Polysilicon.descriptor_pill: 99.9999%+ polysilicon for PV ingots; China holds ~80% glo...
Solar-Grade Polysilicon.about: 99.9999%+ polysilicon for PV ingots; China holds ~80% global capacity.
ai_summary: Purified silicon (6N, 99.9999%) used as the feedstock for solar wafer production — lower purity than electronic grade but produced in vastly larger volumes.
Chinese producers (Tongwei, Daqo, GCL, Xinte) dominate with ~90% of global capacity, driving prices down to $6–8/kg from peaks above $30/kg in 2022.
Produced by the same Siemens process as electronic grade, but with less stringent distillation — or by the lower-cost fluidized bed reactor (FBR) method.
Feeds into the solar panel chain that powers AI datacenters — each GW of solar capacity requires roughly 3,000–4,000 tonnes of polysilicon.
Massive Chinese overcapacity has crashed prices and pushed Western producers (Wacker, Hemlock) to focus on the higher-margin electronic grade.

Silicon Metal (Metallurgical Grade).name: Silicon Metal (Metallurgical Grade)
Silicon Metal (Metallurgical Grade).descriptor_pill: 98%+ silicon from carbothermic reduction of quartzite; fe...
Silicon Metal (Metallurgical Grade).about: 98%+ silicon from carbothermic reduction of quartzite; feedstock for all polysilicon.
ai_summary: Crude silicon (98–99% pure) produced by reducing quartz with carbon in submerged arc furnaces — the first industrial step from rock to silicon.
Major producers include Elkem (Norway), Ferroglobe (US/Spain), and Chinese smelters — production is energy-intensive at ~11 MWh per tonne.
Feeds into both the semiconductor chain (via trichlorosilane purification to polysilicon) and the aluminum alloy chain (as a casting additive).
Global production is roughly 3.5 million t/yr, with China producing ~70% — a large market by specialty metal standards.
Metallurgical silicon is the common ancestor of every chip and every solar cell — abundant but energy-intensive to produce.

High-Purity Quartz.name: High-Purity Quartz
High-Purity Quartz.descriptor_pill: Crucibles for ingot growth and feedstock for fiber-optic ...
High-Purity Quartz.about: Crucibles for ingot growth and feedstock for fiber-optic glass; Spruce Pine NC near-monopoly on top grades.
stats: Sibelco, The Quartz Corp, Norwegian Crystallites
ai_summary: Quartzite ore refined to >99.99% SiO₂ purity — the crucible and tube material used in semiconductor crystal growth and the feedstock for fused quartz optics.
Spruce Pine, North Carolina is the world's dominant source of the highest-purity quartz, supplying crucibles for silicon crystal pulling at every major wafer fab.
A January 2025 landslide near Spruce Pine temporarily disrupted access, highlighting extreme geographic concentration in a material the entire chip industry depends on.
Unimin/Covia (now Sibelco) and The Quartz Corp are the primary processors — the entire semiconductor-grade quartz supply chain runs through a small number of facilities.
High-purity quartz is the geological chokepoint beneath the silicon chain — every wafer fab depends on crucibles made from a handful of quartzite deposits.

CoWoS Advanced Packaging.name: CoWoS Advanced Packaging
CoWoS Advanced Packaging.about: Chip-on-wafer-on-substrate assembly integrating GPU die, HBM, and silicon interposer; the bottleneck behind every Nvidia GPU.
ai_summary: A way of assembling AI chips where the GPU die and memory stacks are mounted side by side on a thin silicon sheet, then wired together with thousands of microscopic copper connections — the step that turns separate chips into a working AI processor.

The silicon interposer underneath carries the copper wiring between GPU and memory, the ABF substrate connects the package to the server board, and underfill resin locks it all in place — three upstream inputs, each with its own supply constraints.
Only TSMC can do this at scale — they're expanding from ~35,000 wafers/month in late 2024 to a projected 130,000 by end of 2026, and it's still sold out.
Nvidia has booked over 60% of all CoWoS capacity through 2027; Google reportedly cut its TPU target from 4 million to 3 million units because it couldn't get enough.
The constraint on AI chip supply isn't designing faster chips — it's physically assembling them, and CoWoS is where that bottleneck sits.

Silicon Interposer.name: Silicon Interposer
Silicon Interposer.descriptor_pill: Passive silicon layer with TSVs routing signals between G...
Silicon Interposer.about: Passive silicon layer with TSVs routing signals between GPU die and HBM stacks within CoWoS packages.
ai_summary: A thin silicon wafer etched with thousands of microscopic copper channels (through-silicon vias) that sits between the chip dies and the substrate — the wiring layer that lets GPU and HBM talk to each other.
Made using standard semiconductor fab equipment but at older process nodes — the interposer itself doesn't need advanced lithography, just precise copper plating and etching.
TSMC produces most silicon interposers in-house as part of its CoWoS packaging line — interposer supply is effectively gated by CoWoS capacity.
As AI chips grow larger (reticle-limited designs like Nvidia's Blackwell use multi-die configurations), interposer size grows proportionally, consuming more wafer area per package.
Silicon interposers are the physical bridge that makes chiplet-based AI processors possible — without them, GPU and memory can't communicate at terabyte-per-second bandwidth.

TSV Copper.name: TSV Copper
TSV Copper.descriptor_pill: Through-silicon-via electroplated copper plugs creating v...
TSV Copper.about: Through-silicon-via electroplated copper plugs creating vertical interconnect in HBM and interposers.
ai_summary: Ultra-pure copper electroplated into vertical holes drilled through silicon wafers — the conductive fills inside through-silicon vias that connect chip layers in 3D packages.
Starts with standard copper cathode but must be deposited with sub-micron uniformity inside high-aspect-ratio holes — a specialized electrochemistry process.
Used in both silicon interposers (for CoWoS) and HBM stacks (connecting stacked DRAM dies) — two of the tightest bottlenecks in AI chip packaging.
TSV copper plating is performed by TSMC, ASE, and Amkor as part of their packaging operations — capacity scales with advanced packaging investment.
A specialized form of a common metal — the constraint isn't copper supply but the precision with which it must be deposited inside microscopic holes.

ABF Substrate.name: ABF Substrate
ABF Substrate.descriptor_pill: Ajinomoto Build-up Film organic substrate carrying GPU/CP...
ABF Substrate.about: Ajinomoto Build-up Film organic substrate carrying GPU/CPU packages; Ajinomoto holds ~95% of the material.
ai_summary: A build-up film made by Ajinomoto (the Japanese food company) that forms the high-density wiring layers connecting chip packages to server boards — the bridge between silicon and PCB.
Ajinomoto holds ~95% market share in ABF film; the material is laminated onto substrates by companies like Ibiden, Shinko, and Unimicron who build the finished package substrates.
Supply-demand turned tight in late 2025, with the shortfall projected to reach 10% in H2 2026 and widen to 42% by 2028 as AI chip packaging demand compounds.
Every GPU, CPU, and networking ASIC in an AI datacenter sits on an ABF substrate — there is no alternative material at the required wiring density.
A food-science company's specialty chemical is the quiet chokepoint beneath every AI chip — Ajinomoto's capacity decisions ripple through the entire semiconductor industry.

FR-4 / High-Speed Laminate.name: FR-4 / High-Speed Laminate
FR-4 / High-Speed Laminate.descriptor_pill: Glass-reinforced epoxy boards forming the bulk of server ...
FR-4 / High-Speed Laminate.about: Glass-reinforced epoxy boards forming the bulk of server and switch PCBs.
ai_summary: Fiberglass cloth impregnated with epoxy resin, pressed into flat sheets, and clad with copper foil — the base material of every printed circuit board in a datacenter.
Upstream inputs are epichlorohydrin (for epoxy), fiberglass woven from silica, and copper foil — all commodity chemicals assembled into a precision composite.
Standard FR-4 handles most applications; high-speed laminates (Megtron, Panasonic) are required for server boards running above 25 Gbps per lane.
Every server board, switch line card, power supply, and networking card in a datacenter is built on FR-4 or its high-speed variants.
PCB laminate is one of the most structurally ubiquitous inputs in electronics — not constrained in commodity grades but tightening at high-speed specifications.

EUV Photoresist.name: EUV Photoresist
EUV Photoresist.descriptor_pill: Tin-oxide cluster light-sensitive films enabling sub-7 nm...
EUV Photoresist.about: Tin-oxide cluster light-sensitive films enabling sub-7 nm patterning on advanced logic and HBM base die.
ai_summary: Light-sensitive polymer coating applied to silicon wafers before exposure to extreme ultraviolet (13.5nm) light — the material that captures chip patterns at the smallest dimensions.
Japanese companies JSR, TOK, and Shin-Etsu Chemical hold ~90% of the EUV photoresist market — production requires atomic-level purity control.
JSR is building a new factory in Taiwan to supply TSMC directly; TOK is investing $130M in a South Korea plant — both targeting capacity by 2028–2030.
Every advanced AI chip (5nm and below) requires EUV lithography, and each exposure layer consumes a fresh coating of EUV photoresist.
EUV photoresist is the chemical that makes sub-5nm chips possible — a Japanese-dominated supply chain feeding the world's most advanced fabs.

DUV Photoresist.name: DUV Photoresist
DUV Photoresist.descriptor_pill: ArF and KrF chemically-amplified resists for 7nm+ and mat...
DUV Photoresist.about: ArF and KrF chemically-amplified resists for 7nm+ and mature nodes including DRAM and NAND.
ai_summary: Light-sensitive polymer for deep ultraviolet (193nm/248nm) lithography — the workhorse patterning chemistry used for mature-node and non-critical layers on advanced chips.
Same Japanese suppliers (JSR, TOK, Shin-Etsu) dominate, but the market is larger and more diversified than EUV resist.
Used on every wafer at every fab worldwide — advanced chips use DUV for non-critical layers even when EUV handles the finest features.
Consumes neon gas in the excimer laser source — the 2022 Ukraine supply shock demonstrated the neon-DUV dependency.
DUV photoresist is the volume backbone of chip patterning — less exotic than EUV but consumed in far greater quantities across more process steps.

CMP Slurries.name: CMP Slurries
CMP Slurries.about: Chemical-mechanical polishing slurries planarizing wafers between layers; ceria, silica, or alumina-based.
ai_summary: Abrasive liquid mixtures used to polish wafer surfaces flat between deposition steps — the process that keeps each layer of a chip planar enough for the next layer to be built on top.
Cerium oxide is the primary abrasive for oxide polishing; silica and alumina slurries handle metal and barrier layers — each step uses a different formulation.
Cabot Microelectronics (now CMC Materials, acquired by Entegris), Fujimi, and Hitachi Chemical are leading suppliers.
Advanced AI chips require more CMP steps per wafer because 3D structures (HBM, CFET) and tighter tolerances demand more frequent planarization.
CMP slurry is a consumable at every fab — demand scales directly with wafer starts and chip complexity.

NdFeB Magnets.name: NdFeB Magnets
NdFeB Magnets.descriptor_pill: Sintered neodymium-iron-boron permanent magnets in HDD vo...
NdFeB Magnets.about: Sintered neodymium-iron-boron permanent magnets in HDD voice coils, fans, wind turbines, EUV stages.
ai_summary: Sintered neodymium-iron-boron permanent magnets — the strongest commercial magnets, used in every motor, fan, and hard drive actuator in a datacenter.
Made by powder metallurgy: rare earth alloy is melted, milled to micron-sized powder, pressed in a magnetic field, and sintered at ~1,000°C — a complex, multi-step process.
China produces ~85% of global NdFeB magnets; April 2025 export controls on dysprosium and terbium — the additives that make high-temp grades work — disrupted Western supply chains.
AI datacenters consume NdFeB magnets in HDD spindle motors, cooling fan motors, wind turbine generators, and precision servo actuators for robotics.
European NdFeB magnet prices reached 6x Chinese domestic levels after the April 2025 controls — the widest spread in the magnet market's history.

InP Wafers.name: InP Wafers
InP Wafers.descriptor_pill: Indium phosphide substrates underlying every high-speed l...
InP Wafers.about: Indium phosphide substrates underlying every high-speed laser and photodiode in 800G/1.6T transceivers.
ai_summary: Crystalline indium phosphide wafers that form the substrate for high-speed laser diodes and photodetectors — the semiconductor material inside every optical transceiver in an AI datacenter.
Grown by the vertical gradient freeze method from high-purity indium and phosphorus — crystal growth is slow and yield-sensitive, limiting throughput.
Sumitomo Electric, AXT, and JX Nippon Mining produce most InP substrates — a small market (~$300M/yr) enabling tens of billions in downstream optical products.
Each transceiver generation (400G → 800G → 1.6T) uses more InP per device as laser arrays grow more complex — demand is scaling faster than wafer supply.
InP wafers are the substrate bottleneck for optical transceivers — McKinsey projects 800G transceivers will fall 40–60% short of demand through 2027.

GaAs Wafers.name: GaAs Wafers
GaAs Wafers.descriptor_pill: Gallium arsenide substrates for 850 nm VCSELs in short-re...
GaAs Wafers.about: Gallium arsenide substrates for 850 nm VCSELs in short-reach optics and RF/analog ICs.
ai_summary: Crystalline gallium arsenide substrates used for laser diodes, RF amplifiers, and LED chips — the compound semiconductor that converts electricity to light.
Grown from high-purity gallium and arsenic using Czochralski or vertical Bridgman methods — toxic arsine gas handling limits the number of qualified manufacturers.
Sumitomo Electric, AXT, and Freiberger Compound Materials are leading substrate producers — a market dominated by a handful of specialized crystal growers.
In AI datacenters, GaAs lasers sit inside every optical transceiver converting electrical signals to light pulses for rack-to-rack communication.
GaAs competes with InP at longer wavelengths and is being partially displaced by silicon photonics, but remains the standard for many transceiver designs.

GaN Wafers.name: GaN Wafers
GaN Wafers.descriptor_pill: Gallium nitride epitaxial wafers (on Si or SiC) for high-...
GaN Wafers.about: Gallium nitride epitaxial wafers (on Si or SiC) for high-efficiency power switches in PSUs and inverters.
ai_summary: Crystalline gallium nitride substrates used for high-power, high-frequency transistors — the material behind the power chips converting voltage in datacenter power supplies.
GaN-on-silicon wafers (cheaper, larger) are displacing GaN-on-SiC for most power applications; true bulk GaN substrates remain expensive and small.
GaN power devices are more efficient than silicon MOSFETs at the voltages used in datacenter PSUs (48V bus, 800V EV charging), reducing waste heat.
Wolfspeed, Infineon, and GaN Systems (now Infineon) are major GaN device makers; upstream wafer supply depends on gallium from Chinese bauxite refining.
GaN power chips are scaling into AI datacenter power delivery — every efficiency point gained at the power supply reduces the cooling load downstream.

Germanium Tetrachloride (GeCl4).name: Germanium Tetrachloride (GeCl4)
Germanium Tetrachloride (GeCl4).descriptor_pill: Refractive-index-raising dopant in fiber-optic glass core...
Germanium Tetrachloride (GeCl4).about: Refractive-index-raising dopant in fiber-optic glass cores; also feeds IR optics, SiGe, and PET catalysis.
ai_summary: Volatile liquid compound of germanium and chlorine — vaporized inside a preform deposition chamber to dope the glass core of fiber optic cables, controlling the refractive index that guides light.
Upstream germanium is refined from zinc smelting byproducts and converted to GeCl₄ at 8N purity — only Umicore in Belgium can do this at commercial scale outside China and Russia.
China's export ban on germanium to the US (late 2024, suspended late 2025) demonstrated how a single policy decision can shut off the fiber optic supply chain.
Every kilometer of standard single-mode fiber optic cable requires ~0.12 grams of germanium delivered as GeCl₄.
GeCl₄ is the molecular bottleneck between germanium supply and fiber optic cable production — the chokepoint where mineral scarcity converts to infrastructure constraint.

Nickel Single-Crystal Superalloy.name: Nickel Single-Crystal Superalloy
Nickel Single-Crystal Superalloy.descriptor_pill: Ni-based alloy with Re/Co/W/Ta/Hf used in gas turbine hot...
Nickel Single-Crystal Superalloy.about: Ni-based alloy with Re/Co/W/Ta/Hf used in gas turbine hot-section blades and vanes.
ai_summary: Nickel-based alloy grown as a single crystal to eliminate grain boundaries — the material that withstands 1,400°C+ gas turbine inlet temperatures without creeping or cracking.
Alloyed with chromium, cobalt, tungsten, rhenium, hafnium, and aluminum in precise ratios — each element serves a specific metallurgical function in the crystal structure.
Cast as single crystals in directionally solidified investment casting furnaces — Precision Castparts (Berkshire Hathaway), Howmet, and Rolls-Royce are leading casters.
Every gas turbine blade in the hot section of a frame or aeroderivative turbine powering an AI datacenter is made from this alloy.

Single-crystal superalloys sit at the intersection of seven upstream metals — rhenium, hafnium, tungsten, cobalt, chromium, nickel, and aluminum — making turbine blades one of the most material-intensive components in the chain.

Stainless Steel.name: Stainless Steel
Stainless Steel.descriptor_pill: 316-grade plate, tube, and fittings throughout cooling lo...
Stainless Steel.about: 316-grade plate, tube, and fittings throughout cooling loops, CDUs, and heat exchangers.
ai_summary: Iron-chromium alloy (minimum 10.5% Cr) with corrosion resistance — the standard material for datacenter cooling piping, heat exchangers, and chemical-resistant structures.
316-grade stainless (16–18% chromium, 10–14% nickel, 2–3% molybdenum) is the workhorse specification for datacenter thermal systems.
Global stainless steel production exceeds 60 million t/yr, with China producing ~55% — supply is generally adequate.
Every chilled water loop, coolant distribution system, and heat exchanger in a datacenter uses stainless steel piping and fittings.
Stainless steel is a bulk infrastructure material — widely available but consuming meaningful quantities of nickel, chromium, and molybdenum per datacenter.

Grain-Oriented Electrical Steel.name: Grain-Oriented Electrical Steel
Grain-Oriented Electrical Steel.descriptor_pill: Specialized silicon steel laminations for transformer cor...
Grain-Oriented Electrical Steel.about: Specialized silicon steel laminations for transformer cores; the bottleneck behind the transformer bottleneck.
ai_summary: Silicon steel sheet with aligned crystal grains that channel magnetic flux efficiently — the core material inside every power transformer in the grid and datacenter.
Produced by a complex rolling and annealing process that aligns iron crystals along the rolling direction — only ~15 mills worldwide can make GOES to transformer specification.
Nippon Steel, POSCO, JFE, and Baosteel dominate production — US capacity is limited, driving transformer lead times to 2–3 years.
Every step-down transformer, generator step-up transformer, and distribution transformer in a datacenter power chain contains a GOES core.
Transformer delivery delays are one of the most binding constraints on AI datacenter energization timelines — and GOES supply is the material bottleneck behind those delays.

LFP Battery Cells.name: LFP Battery Cells
LFP Battery Cells.descriptor_pill: Lithium iron phosphate cells dominating stationary storag...
LFP Battery Cells.about: Lithium iron phosphate cells dominating stationary storage for UPS and BESS.
ai_summary: Lithium iron phosphate cells — the rechargeable battery chemistry dominating datacenter energy storage because of superior cycle life, thermal stability, and lower cost per kWh than NMC.
Cathode is made from iron phosphate and lithium carbonate upstream; anode is graphite; electrolyte is a lithium salt dissolved in organic solvent.
CATL, BYD, and EVE Energy produce ~80% of global LFP cells — Chinese dominance in cell manufacturing is even more extreme than in raw materials.
LFP now holds ~90% of the BESS market globally; datacenter installations typically deploy 2–4 hour systems at 100+ MWh scale.
LFP cells are ~40% cheaper than NMC in 2025 and cycle 3–4x longer — the economics have made them the default for every new datacenter battery installation.

LFP Cathode Active Material.name: LFP Cathode Active Material
LFP Cathode Active Material.descriptor_pill: Lithium iron phosphate cathode powder; China holds ~95% p...
LFP Cathode Active Material.about: Lithium iron phosphate cathode powder; China holds ~95% production capacity.
ai_summary: Lithium iron phosphate powder (LiFePO₄) — the cathode material that stores and releases lithium ions inside every LFP battery cell.
Made by reacting iron phosphate precursor with lithium carbonate at high temperature — a process requiring precise stoichiometry and particle size control.
China produces ~95% of global LFP cathode material — even Western cell manufacturers (Gotion, FREYR) source cathode from Chinese precursor suppliers.
Iron and phosphorus feedstocks are individually abundant; the constraint is the integrated processing chain that converts them to battery-grade LFP powder.
LFP cathode is where Chinese processing dominance is most extreme in the battery chain — the chokepoint is chemistry, not geology.

Lithium Carbonate.name: Lithium Carbonate
Lithium Carbonate.descriptor_pill: Battery-grade Li2CO3 from brine or hard rock; precursor t...
Lithium Carbonate.about: Battery-grade Li2CO3 from brine or hard rock; precursor to all lithium cathode chemistries.
ai_summary: White powder (Li₂CO₃) that provides the lithium for LFP and NMC cathode synthesis — the most traded form of battery-grade lithium.
Extracted from Chilean/Argentinian brine evaporation or Australian spodumene hard-rock mining, then refined to battery grade (>99.5% purity).
Prices collapsed from ~$80/kg in late 2022 to ~$10–15/kg by mid-2025, driven by Chinese refining overcapacity and slower-than-expected EV adoption.
Every MWh of LFP battery storage at an AI datacenter requires roughly 100–150 kg of lithium carbonate equivalent.
Lithium is in temporary surplus, but the compounding demand from EVs and datacenter BESS means the current price trough is likely cyclical, not structural.

Battery-Grade Graphite.name: Battery-Grade Graphite
Battery-Grade Graphite.descriptor_pill: Coated synthetic and natural graphite anode material; ~70...
Battery-Grade Graphite.about: Coated synthetic and natural graphite anode material; ~70% China-processed.
ai_summary: Spherical graphite processed from natural flake graphite or synthesized from petroleum coke — the anode material in virtually all lithium-ion batteries.
China controls ~90% of spherical graphite processing — the shaping, coating, and purification steps that convert raw flake into battery-ready material.
Each GWh of LFP battery storage requires roughly 800–1,000 tonnes of anode graphite — volumes scale directly with datacenter BESS deployment.
China imposed export licensing on graphite in late 2023; US and EU have added graphite to critical mineral lists and are funding domestic processing capacity.
Graphite is the anode chokepoint that mirrors lithium on the cathode side — Chinese processing dominance is even more concentrated.

Battery Electrolyte.name: Battery Electrolyte
Battery Electrolyte.descriptor_pill: LiPF6 in carbonate solvents enabling lithium-ion conducti...
Battery Electrolyte.about: LiPF6 in carbonate solvents enabling lithium-ion conduction inside cells.
ai_summary: Lithium salt (typically LiPF₆) dissolved in organic carbonates — the ion-conducting liquid inside every lithium-ion battery cell.
Production requires high-purity lithium hexafluorophosphate synthesis, which uses hydrofluoric acid and lithium carbonate as feedstocks — a hazardous chemical process.
Chinese suppliers (Tinci Materials, Do-Fluoride) dominate global electrolyte production — non-Chinese capacity is limited.
Electrolyte quality directly affects cell performance, safety, and cycle life — contamination at parts-per-million levels can cause premature failure.
Electrolyte is the liquid that makes lithium-ion chemistry work — less discussed than cathode or anode but equally essential and equally China-dependent.

Vanadium Redox Electrolyte.name: Vanadium Redox Electrolyte
Vanadium Redox Electrolyte.descriptor_pill: Vanadium sulfate solution storing energy in redox flow ba...
Vanadium Redox Electrolyte.about: Vanadium sulfate solution storing energy in redox flow batteries; same vanadium cycles for 25+ years.
ai_summary: Vanadium dissolved in sulfuric acid at two oxidation states — the energy-storing liquid that flows through vanadium redox flow battery (VRFB) stacks.
Made by dissolving vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) in sulfuric acid — the electrolyte doesn't degrade over time, which is the core advantage of flow batteries.
Invinity Energy Systems, Rongke Power, and CellCube are leading VRFB manufacturers using this electrolyte chemistry.
VRFBs offer 4–8 hour discharge with near-unlimited cycle life — well-suited to long-duration datacenter grid storage where lithium-ion degrades too fast.
