Scrap Steel.descriptor_pill: Recycled feedstock for EAF steelmaking; ~70% of US struct...
Scrap Steel.about: Recycled feedstock for EAF steelmaking; ~70% of US structural steel input.
ai_summary: Recycled steel collected from demolished structures, end-of-life vehicles, and manufacturing offcuts — the primary feedstock for electric arc furnace (EAF) steelmaking.
Global scrap steel trade is roughly 100 million t/yr, with the US as the world's largest scrap exporter.
EAF steelmaking (scrap-based) produces ~30% of global steel and has a ~75% lower carbon footprint than blast furnace steelmaking.
Structural steel for datacenter construction increasingly sources from EAF mills to meet corporate sustainability commitments.
Nucor and Steel Dynamics dominate US EAF steelmaking — the companies most likely to supply domestic datacenter structural steel.
Scrap steel is the circular-economy input to datacenter construction — abundant, lower-carbon, and increasingly preferred by hyperscaler procurement teams.

Coking Coal.name: Coking Coal
Coking Coal.descriptor_pill: Metallurgical coal reducing iron ore in blast furnaces an...
Coking Coal.about: Metallurgical coal reducing iron ore in blast furnaces and feeding silicon-metal furnaces.
ai_summary: Metallurgical coal heated in the absence of air to produce coke — the carbon-rich fuel and reducing agent used in blast furnace steelmaking.
Global production is roughly 1.1 billion t/yr, with China, Australia, and the US as leading producers.
Each tonne of blast furnace steel requires roughly 0.6 tonnes of coking coal — a direct physical input that cannot be substituted at scale.
Australia dominates the seaborne coking coal market, with BHP, Glencore, and Anglo American as major exporters.
Coking coal is not consumed in EAF steelmaking, which uses scrap — the coal dependency exists only in the blast furnace route.
Coking coal's role in AI infrastructure is one step removed — it makes the steel that frames the buildings, relevant only where blast furnace steel is sourced.

Zinc.name: Zinc
Zinc.descriptor_pill: Galvanizing on structural and cold-formed steel; cadmium ...
Zinc.about: Galvanizing on structural and cold-formed steel; cadmium and indium are zinc byproducts.
ai_summary: Base metal used primarily for galvanizing steel against corrosion — the protective coating on structural steel in virtually every building.
Global mine production is roughly 13 million t/yr, led by China, Australia, and Peru.
In AI infrastructure, zinc appears as galvanized coatings on datacenter structural steel, roofing, and cable trays.
Zinc smelting is also the upstream source of germanium and indium byproducts — the same smelters that galvanize steel produce fiber optic feedstock.
Zinc prices have been range-bound at $1.00–1.30/lb through 2024–2025, with smelter treatment charges compressing refiner margins.
Zinc's AI infrastructure thesis is indirect but real — it is the host metal whose smelting byproducts include two of the most supply-constrained trace elements in the chain.

Cement.name: Cement
Cement.descriptor_pill: Volume-dominant binder for foundation pours and slabs; ma...
Cement.about: Volume-dominant binder for foundation pours and slabs; major embodied-carbon line item.
ai_summary: Powdered calcium silicate produced by heating limestone and clay in rotary kilns at ~1,450°C — the binder in all concrete.
Global production exceeds 4 billion t/yr, with China producing ~55% — the most-produced manufactured material on Earth.
Every AI datacenter foundation, slab, and structural element uses reinforced concrete — a typical 100 MW facility requires 50,000–100,000 cubic yards.
Cement production generates ~8% of global CO₂ emissions, making it a focus of hyperscaler Scope 3 accounting.
Low-carbon cement alternatives (CarbonCure, Solidia, Holcim ECOPact) are gaining traction in datacenter construction specifications.
Cement is a bulk commodity that every datacenter sits on — not a supply constraint but an emissions hotspot that sustainability-focused operators increasingly manage.

Aggregates.name: Aggregates
Aggregates.descriptor_pill: Sand, gravel, and crushed stone bulking out concrete and ...
Aggregates.about: Sand, gravel, and crushed stone bulking out concrete and base layers.
stats: Vulcan Materials, Martin Marietta, Heidelberg Materials
ai_summary: Crushed stone, gravel, and sand mixed with cement to form concrete — the filler material in every concrete pour.
Global production exceeds 40 billion tonnes per year, making aggregates the most extracted natural resource on Earth.
A 100 MW datacenter construction typically consumes 100,000–200,000 tonnes of aggregates for foundations, floors, and access roads.
Supply is locally sourced due to high weight-to-value ratio — transportation costs dominate economics, not material scarcity.
Sand shortages have emerged in some coastal and riverine regions, but aggregate supply for inland datacenter construction is generally adequate.
Aggregates are the most voluminous input in the entire AI infrastructure chain — structurally present in vast quantities but not a meaningful constraint.

Water.name: Water
Water.descriptor_pill: Cooling tower makeup, fab ultra-pure-water feedstock, and...
Water.about: Cooling tower makeup, fab ultra-pure-water feedstock, and concrete mixing; major siting constraint.
ai_summary: The universal solvent and coolant — consumed in enormous quantities at every stage of the AI infrastructure supply chain.
A 100 MW air-cooled datacenter can consume 1–5 million gallons of water per day for evaporative cooling, depending on climate.
Ultra-pure water (UPW, 18.2 MΩ·cm resistivity) is consumed at every semiconductor fab — roughly 2,000–5,000 gallons per wafer.
Water scarcity is reshaping datacenter siting decisions — desert locations with cheap power now face community opposition over water consumption.
Liquid cooling (direct-to-chip) reduces evaporative water consumption by 80–90% compared to air cooling with wet economizers.
Water is the most fundamental constraint on datacenter geography that isn't electricity — the resource that determines where AI can physically be built.

Natural Gas.name: Natural Gas
Natural Gas.descriptor_pill: Primary fuel for behind-the-meter turbines, recip engines...
Natural Gas.about: Primary fuel for behind-the-meter turbines, recip engines, fuel cells; also a chemical feedstock.
ai_summary: Fossil fuel burned in gas turbines for electricity generation and used as feedstock for hydrogen, ammonia, and petrochemical production.
Global production exceeds 4 trillion cubic meters per year, with the US, Russia, and Qatar as top producers.
Natural gas turbines are the dominant onsite power solution for AI datacenters that cannot wait for grid interconnection or nuclear permitting.
Combined-cycle gas turbine (CCGT) plants can deliver 500+ MW to a single datacenter campus within 18–24 months of groundbreaking.
Henry Hub prices have traded $2–4/MMBtu through 2024–2025, making gas the cheapest dispatchable power source for US datacenters.
Gas is the bridge fuel powering the first wave of GW-scale AI datacenters — the question is how long the bridge needs to be before nuclear and renewables catch up.

Crude Oil.name: Crude Oil
Crude Oil.descriptor_pill: Refined into diesel for backup gensets and petrochemical ...
Crude Oil.about: Refined into diesel for backup gensets and petrochemical feedstock for plastics and resins.
ai_summary: Primary fossil fuel refined into diesel, jet fuel, lubricants, and the petrochemical feedstocks used in plastics, resins, and synthetic materials.
Global production is roughly 100 million barrels per day, with the US, Saudi Arabia, and Russia as the top three producers.
In AI infrastructure, crude oil derivatives appear as diesel for backup generators, lubricants for cooling systems, and feedstock for all synthetic polymers.
Every datacenter maintains diesel fuel reserves for backup power — typically 24–72 hours of fuel at full load.
Crude oil prices have traded in the $70–90/bbl range through 2024–2025 (Brent), with OPEC+ managing supply.
Crude oil's datacenter role is structural but declining — as battery backup and gas turbines replace diesel generators, the direct linkage weakens.

Diesel Fuel.name: Diesel Fuel
Diesel Fuel.descriptor_pill: Backup-generator fuel with multi-day on-site storage; ref...
Diesel Fuel.about: Backup-generator fuel with multi-day on-site storage; refined from crude oil.
ai_summary: Middle distillate fuel refined from crude oil — the standard fuel for datacenter backup generators worldwide.
Global diesel consumption is roughly 28 million barrels per day, with the US, China, and India as top consumers.
Every Tier III and Tier IV datacenter maintains diesel generators sized to carry full facility load during grid outages.
A 100 MW datacenter typically stores 500,000–1,000,000 gallons of diesel onsite for 24–72 hours of backup runtime.
Battery energy storage systems (BESS) are beginning to displace diesel for short-duration backup, but diesel remains the standard for extended outages.
Diesel is the last-resort power source for AI infrastructure — being gradually displaced by BESS and gas turbines but still universally deployed.
